title: AI is coming for BigLaw grads: What shrinking intakes mean for Australia's future lawyers
author: Lawyers Weekly

dom.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source supplies a narrow reported example of AI-linked graduate hiring cuts, consistent with the cluster’s observation that workforce effects may differ by setting. However, it provides no figures or independent causal evidence and does not address the cluster’s principal proposition about multidisciplinary implementation, verification, task-specific evaluation or reliable service delivery.
qs: Australia’s legal profession is entering a pivotal turning point as AI begins reshaping one of the industry’s most traditional career pipelines: graduate recruitment.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks

This materially strengthens the cluster’s account of concentrated junior pressure while preserving its caution that profession-wide displacement and broader replication remain unestablished.

kp.k: MinterEllison links graduate hiring cuts to AI efficiency
kp.d: The May 20, 2026 article reports that MinterEllison reduced graduate hires from 104 to 72 for the 2025–26 cycle, nearly a third. Chief people officer Rachel Banks, quoted from The Australian Financial Review, attributes the more targeted intake to AI improving efficiency in routine graduate work alongside demand shifting towards complex matters. The article acknowledges that recruitment numbers fluctuate annually; the distinctive feature is the firm's stated explanation.
qs: Top-tier law firm MinterEllison has cut nearly a third of its graduate intake, reducing hires from 104 to 72 for the 2025–26 cycle, with the firm publicly linking the move to the growing impact of AI on legal work.
While graduate recruitment numbers fluctuate from year to year, the significance of MinterEllison’s announcement lies in its reasoning.

Responsible use of AI is improving efficiency in some of the more routine work graduates traditionally start on, while demand continues to shift towards complex matters. That combination has led us to take a more targeted approach to intake this year,

kp.k: Shrinking intakes threaten confidence in traditional entry pathways
kp.d: Recent graduate and law clerk Liberty Papas describes uncertainty surrounding the traditional BigLaw route and predicts increased pressure over grades, experience and early career planning if opportunities become scarcer. Sydney Law School dean Fleur Johns also reports student anxiety about changing market conditions and says the school is taking supportive steps. These are interviewees' observations and expectations rather than measured student outcomes.
qs: When these firms begin signalling reductions in graduate intakes, students inevitably begin questioning what that means for their future prospects.
I think it can amplify pressure around grades, work experience, and whether students have ‘done enough’ to be competitive,

There is already a strong culture around maintaining competitive grades, securing legal experience early and building a résumé from first year onwards. If opportunities become more limited, students may feel they need to distinguish themselves even further.
It means that law students are experiencing anxiety about changing market conditions; we are very conscious of that and taking steps to ensure students feel supported,

kp.k: Educators prioritise durable analytical and human capabilities
kp.d: University of Melbourne associate professor Jake Goldenfein argues against overemphasising technical systems that will become obsolete, instead prioritising critical capacity and the foundations of legal analysis while preparing students for different workplace demands. Johns expresses confidence in future Sydney Law School employment outcomes based on transferable capabilities including complex problem solving, communication, judgement, leadership and legal innovation. Her confidence is prospective, not a reported employment finding.
qs: We don’t want to overly focus on the use of technical systems that will inevitably become obsolete, but we still need to prepare students for a different kind of workplace that values different kinds of skills,
For us, that means making sure students have extremely sharp critical capacity and understand the hierarchies of knowledge that underpin good legal analysis.

Nevertheless, we are confident that students graduating from Sydney Law School in coming years will continue to enjoy a wide range of career options and attain sector-leading levels of graduate employment,

The capabilities for complex problem solving, human communication, discerning judgement, leadership, and legal innovation that students can build in this law school put them in a very strong position to weather these changing conditions successfully.

kp.k: Alternative pathways may offer earlier practical responsibility
kp.d: Papas argues that boutique firms, government, community legal centres and specialised practices can provide earlier responsibility and practical exposure than larger graduate programmes. Drawing on her own experience, she emphasises relationships, mentorship and practical exposure alongside academic achievement. Her comparison of pathways is a practitioner perspective, not a quantified assessment of training outcomes.
qs: Over time, though, my perspective shifted because my own pathway looked different. My opportunity came through genuine relationships, mentorship, and practical exposure,

At the time, I remember feeling self-conscious that I had not followed the same trajectory as many of my peers. Looking back now, I realise that experience, networking and people who believe in you can be just as important as academic results.
Boutique firms, government positions, community legal centres and specialised practices can provide earlier responsibility and more hands-on exposure.
In many cases, students may actually gain practical experience sooner and develop stronger professional skills than they would through a larger graduate structure.

kp.k: Advisers recommend broadening legal career ambitions
kp.d: College of Law career adviser Susan Pincus recommends considering government, smaller firms, in-house legal counsel, new law and overseas work, as well as adjacent careers in policy, law reform, consulting and start-ups. Johns suggests that hiring changes may encourage a beneficial broader perspective, noting that relatively few law graduates pursue BigLaw careers long term without supplying a percentage. These are recommendations and anticipated responses to changing opportunities.
qs: Law students need to be more informed and aware of other options beyond the more traditional pathways of joining big law firms,
These may include alternatives such as government, smaller firms, in-house legal counsel, new law, or even doing an overseas stint.
In addition, there are a number of career options that draw off a law degree, such as adjacent roles in legal policy and law reform, consulting, entrepreneurial start-ups, etc,
Considering the relatively small percentage of law graduates who actually pursue careers in ‘BigLaw’ long term, a shift towards a wider-angle perspective could be a good thing.
In some ways, this can be seen as a wake-up call to students that they need to be versatile and resourceful to ensure they do not get left behind,

kp.k: Wider hiring cuts remain uncertain; adaptability gains emphasis
kp.d: Goldenfein considers it very possible that other BigLaw firms will follow MinterEllison, but stresses that AI-related workplace economics remain unsettled. He also anticipates diverse forms of AI engagement across employment pathways. Separately, Pincus reports Gilbert + Tobin CEO Sam Nickless's emphasis on securing AI-native talent early and recruiting for intelligence, curiosity and adaptability. This reported hiring preference does not establish an industry-wide reduction in graduate recruitment.
qs: Against that backdrop, and while only time will tell, Goldenfein suggested it is “very possible”, explaining how the “economics of the workplace in the context of AI are still taking shape”.
There are a range of employment pathways that inevitably involve engagement with AI in diverse ways and for different reasons.
“Sam Nickless, Gilbert + Tobin’s CEO, states ‘Securing top talent early, who have come through in an ‘AI-native’ world, is a priority for us’,” Pincus said.
Their firm looks for graduates with ‘raw smarts plus curiosity’, particularly with the ability to adapt to a rapidly changing world.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: AI-enabled efficiency in routine junior work is linked to a smaller MinterEllison graduate intake; wider BigLaw hiring reductions are presented as possible, not established.
pts.d: Grace Robbie reports that MinterEllison reduced its graduate intake from 104 to 72 for the 2025–26 cycle and publicly linked the reduction to AI. The firm's explanation combines efficiency in routine graduate work with a shift in demand towards complex matters, rather than identifying AI as the sole cause. Interviewee Jake Goldenfein describes similar moves by other BigLaw firms as 'very possible', while stressing that AI-related workplace economics remain unsettled. The article documents reduced recruitment, not layoffs or a measured profession-wide decline. MinterEllison is the Australian law firm discussed here, not one of the Big Four accounting networks.

pts.k: Shrinking or potentially shrinking graduate intakes may increase student anxiety, competitive pressure and earlier career planning.
pts.d: Liberty Papas predicts that signals of reduced hiring will make students question the traditional route into practice, intensify comparisons over grades and experience, and encourage earlier efforts to distinguish themselves. Fleur Johns reports that students are already anxious about changing market conditions and that Sydney Law School is taking steps to support them. These are interviewees' observations and conditional predictions, not survey findings demonstrating an AI-specific effect.

pts.k: AI-related workplace change is prompting a reconsideration of graduate skills, with emphasis on durable analytical abilities and adaptability rather than mastery of particular technical systems alone.
pts.d: Goldenfein says universities are reconsidering how to prepare competitive graduates for a workplace valuing different skills, prioritising critical capacity and the foundations of legal analysis because technical systems will become obsolete. He also expects multiple employment pathways to involve AI. Johns predicts continued broad opportunities and strong employment outcomes for Sydney Law School graduates, grounded in transferable human capabilities. Susan Pincus presents AI-native talent and adaptability as recruitment priorities, using remarks she quotes from Gilbert + Tobin's CEO as her example; this is not an independently established sector-wide hiring trend.

pts.k: AI-linked pressure on BigLaw recruitment may redirect graduates towards a wider range of legal and non-legal careers.
pts.d: Johns predicts that students may increasingly seek graduate employment and early training outside large commercial firms, presenting greater awareness of diverse careers as a best-case outcome. Papas reports growing openness to alternatives and suggests that boutique firms, government, community legal centres and specialised practices can provide earlier responsibility and practical development than large graduate programmes. Pincus recommends broader career awareness and greater versatility. These claims concern possible responses to the changing market; the article does not quantify movement into alternative careers or demonstrate that those employers can absorb reduced BigLaw hiring.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of one firm's reported intake reduction and explanation, supplemented by professional opinion, institutional observations and personal experience.
pts.d: The principal numerical evidence is MinterEllison's change from 104 to 72 graduate hires, a reduction of 32. Robbie relays the firm's explanation through a statement reported by The Australian Financial Review. Papas draws on her experience as a recent graduate and law clerk, including her non-traditional entry route. Johns and Goldenfein offer law-school leadership and academic perspectives; Pincus offers career-advisory views and a quoted recruitment example from Gilbert + Tobin. No AI productivity measurements, task-displacement data, multi-firm recruitment series, student survey results or employment forecasts are supplied. Johns's confidence in future employment outcomes is not accompanied by supporting employment statistics.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The concrete recruitment change concerns 2025–26; broader market effects are near-term or open-ended possibilities, and continued graduate success is forecast for the coming years.
pts.d: The article is dated May 20, 2026. MinterEllison's reported reduction applies to the 2025–26 cycle, with its explanation referring to a more targeted intake 'this year'. That explanation is qualified by responsible AI use, efficiency in only some routine work and changing demand for complex matters. Student pressure is partly conditional on opportunities becoming more limited. Other firms following suit has no specified deadline and is explicitly uncertain. Johns's employment outlook concerns Sydney Law School graduates 'in coming years', while broader career diversification is described as a possible, best-case response. No timetable is offered for technical obsolescence or profession-wide restructuring.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The main affected groups are Australian law students and graduates, large commercial firms, and legal educators, with alternative employers presented as potential career destinations.
pts.d: Aspiring BigLaw entrants face fewer positions at the named firm and possible changes to routine-work training opportunities, competition and career planning. Large commercial firms are described as reconsidering intake size and desired graduate capabilities. Law schools face demands for student support and preparation for AI-involving workplaces. Boutique and smaller firms, government, community legal centres, specialised practices, corporate in-house departments and adjacent non-legal fields are identified as alternatives, not as demonstrated sources of AI-driven job growth. The article does not specify effects on client prices, service quality or public access to justice.
